passage:
"Parveen, sit here, you can see both the board and Ms. Nair's hands," Ujjwal said, pulling out a chair in the front row.
Parveen signed a quick thanks. The interpreter, Ms. Nair, was already at the corner.
The lecturer asked a question. Ujjwal started to say, "Tell her—" and stopped himself. He turned and looked at Parveen. "What do you think about the second case?" Then he waited. A few seconds passed while the interpreter finished the sentence.
Parveen signed her answer. Ms. Nair voiced it. The class went quiet, then someone nodded.
"Good point," Ujjwal said, to Parveen and not to the interpreter.
Parveen smiled. Later she signed, slowly, that it was the first time this term a classmate had looked at her, not the interpreter.

qa.q: Where did Ujjwal suggest Parveen sit?
qa.a: He suggested she sit in the front row, where she could see both the board and Ms. Nair's hands.

qa.q: What did Parveen feel when Ujjwal looked at her and waited, and how do you know?
qa.a: She felt included, shown by her smile and by signing that it was the first time this term a classmate had looked at her and not the interpreter.

qa.q: What could other classmates learn from Ujjwal's habit?
qa.a: They could speak to the deaf student directly, look at her, and wait patiently for the interpreter's lag.

qa.q: How might it feel for Parveen when people talk to the interpreter instead of her?
qa.a: It probably feels like being talked about rather than to, so she may feel invisible even though the interpreter is there to help.

grounding: A hearing peer speaks to a deaf student and waits for the interpreter's lag in a classroom.

passage: My name is Indu, and I'd like to describe the day I learned what it is to wait. My classmate Payal is deaf, and our seminar uses a sign language interpreter. For weeks I chatted to the interpreter when I wanted to ask Payal something, like "Ask her if she has the notes." Payal noticed. One afternoon she gave me a small, patient look, and I felt my ears go hot. She wasn't angry, but I understood. The next time I turned to face her, said my question, and then counted quietly while the interpreter signed it. There was a pause. Payal smiled and answered. It felt slower, but it felt more like a conversation. I still catch myself starting to turn to the interpreter sometimes.

qa.q: What did Indu say to the interpreter before changing the habit?
qa.a: Indu said things like "Ask her if she has the notes."

qa.q: What did Indu feel when Payal gave Indu a patient look, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Indu felt embarrassed, since Indu's ears went hot, and realised that Indu had been talking around Payal instead of to her.

qa.q: What could Indu do to keep the new habit?
qa.a: Indu could keep practising facing Payal, speak to her, and wait through the interpreter's lag even when it feels slow.

qa.q: How might the wait feel from Payal's side?
qa.a: Payal may feel respected when Indu waits and looks at her, because it treats her as the person in the conversation.

grounding: Indu learns to speak to a deaf classmate directly and wait for the interpreter.

passage:
Class teacher's note, first-year economics, Monday.
Kamal, a Deaf student, joined our section this term with a sign language interpreter, Ms Farida. In the first week I noticed two problems. When classmates asked Kamal questions, they looked at Ms Farida and said, "Ask him if he has notes." Kamal's face showed he'd noticed. Also, in discussions, people kept talking over each other, and Ms Farida couldn't keep up; Kamal often raised his hand just after the topic had moved on. Today I gave the class two simple rules: speak directly to Kamal, not to the interpreter, and pause a few seconds after a question so the interpretation can catch up. We also turned on captions for videos. In this afternoon's discussion, Irawati asked Kamal directly for his view, then waited. He answered through Ms Farida, and the class actually heard him. I'll check with Kamal next week about what else would help.
— Mr Sen

qa.q: What did Mr Sen turn on for videos?
qa.a: Captions.

qa.q: What might Kamal have been feeling when classmates spoke to the interpreter about him?
qa.a: His face showed he'd noticed, suggesting he felt left out and talked about rather than to.

qa.q: What changes did Mr Sen make, and why do they help?
qa.a: Speaking directly to Kamal, pausing for the interpreter's lag and using captions, so Kamal could join discussions on time.

qa.q: How did Irawati include Kamal in the afternoon discussion?
qa.a: She asked Kamal directly for his view and then waited, so his answer came through before the topic moved on.

grounding: Shows a classroom learning to speak directly to a Deaf student and wait for the interpreter's lag, supported by captions.

passage:
Thursday.
Group project meeting with Santosh today. Santosh is Deaf, and his interpreter, Mrs Rao, came with him. I'm Harsha, and I realised halfway through that I'd been talking to Mrs Rao the whole time, saying things like "Can he do the survey part?" Santosh was sitting right there. He tapped the table and signed, and Mrs Rao said, "I'm right here, Harsha. Ask me." My face burned.
After that I turned to Santosh and asked him directly. I also noticed the gap: Mrs Rao needs a few seconds to interpret. Whenever I asked a question and jumped in again too fast, Santosh missed the chance to answer. So I counted three in my head each time. It felt slow at first, then normal.
By the end, Santosh had taken the survey section and suggested a better sample. Next time I'll send the agenda the night before so he can prepare too.
— Harsha

qa.q: What did Santosh take on in the project?
qa.a: The survey section.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling when Santosh said "I'm right here, Harsha"?
qa.a: Harsha felt embarrassed, face burning, realising Harsha had been talking about Santosh instead of to him.

qa.q: What did Harsha change during the meeting?
qa.a: Harsha spoke directly to Santosh and counted three before speaking again, giving time for the interpreter's lag.

qa.q: How did Santosh respond when Harsha kept talking to the interpreter?
qa.a: He tapped the table and pointed it out through Mrs Rao, asking to be spoken to directly.

grounding: Shows a hearing student learning to speak to a Deaf classmate rather than the interpreter and to wait for the interpreter's lag.

passage:
Farhan: can I tell you something about today's seminar?
Mridul: ya
Farhan: when Prof asked for questions, everyone jumped in immediately. by the time my interpreter finished signing the question, the topic had changed
Farhan: I had my hand up for five minutes
Mridul: oh no. I didn't even notice. sorry
Farhan: not your fault. but it happens every week
Mridul: what would help?
Farhan: honestly? if people wait a few seconds after a question. and if you say things TO me, not to my interpreter. people keep saying "tell him..."
Mridul: I've done that 😔
Mridul: ok. I'll wait. and I'll talk to you directly. also should I tell Prof about the pause?
Farhan: I'll mail her. but if you back me up in class, that would help a lot
Mridul: done. tomorrow I'll literally count to five out loud if I have to 😅

qa.q: How long did Farhan have a hand up in the seminar?
qa.a: For five minutes.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling about the seminar?
qa.a: Farhan felt frustrated and left out, since the discussion moved on before the interpretation caught up, every week.

qa.q: What did Mridul agree to do that helps?
qa.a: Wait a few seconds after questions, speak directly to Farhan instead of the interpreter, and back Farhan up in class.

qa.q: How did Mridul feel on realising the problem?
qa.a: Mridul felt sorry and a bit guilty, admitting to having spoken to the interpreter instead of to Farhan.

grounding: Shows a Deaf student explaining that peers should speak directly to him and wait for the interpreter's lag, and a friend agreeing to help.

passage: At the government college in Solapur, the new interpreter, Mrs Kale, sat beside the blackboard every morning, signing the lectures for Vishal, who was Deaf and the first student there to have one. On Monday, during group work, Deepika turned to Mrs Kale and said, "Ask him if he's done the chemistry assignment." Mrs Kale signed it, and Vishal replied, but his eyes stayed on Deepika, a little flat. Later Mrs Kale took Deepika aside. "Speak to him, not to me. Say 'Have you done it?' and look at him. I'll carry the words." On Thursday Deepika tried. She faced Vishal, asked her question, then waited while Mrs Kale's hands caught up. The pause felt long, three or four seconds, and she almost repeated herself. She didn't. Vishal answered, grinning, and added a joke that took Mrs Kale a moment to translate. When the laugh finally reached Deepika, it landed just as warmly.

qa.q: Who was the interpreter?
qa.a: Mrs Kale.

qa.q: What might Vishal's flat look on Monday suggest?
qa.a: He likely felt talked about rather than talked to, a little hurt or left out, when Deepika addressed the interpreter; it could also have been simple tiredness.

qa.q: What did Deepika change on Thursday?
qa.a: She faced Vishal, spoke to him directly, and waited through the interpreter's lag instead of repeating herself.

qa.q: How did Mrs Kale see her own role?
qa.a: As someone who carries the words rather than a partner in the conversation, which is why she asked Deepika to speak to Vishal.

grounding: It illustrates a hearing student learning to speak to a Deaf classmate rather than to the interpreter, and to wait for the interpreter's lag.
